meaningful_reference_text: Return to the branch manager. If the bad quarter was two standard deviations below average and the same illustrative correlation of 0.40 applied, the model would predict the next quarter at 0.8 standard deviations below average without any managerial change. That is a visible recovery of 1.2 standard deviations. @fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage shows the corresponding geometry. The recovery can be real while its attribution to the rescue plan remains unproven. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.

Each requires a different comparison, as @tbl-confidence-calibration shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.

The **planning fallacy** illustrates how optimistic forecasts can affect a project: people often construct an inside-view story of the steps that should occur while underweighting delays observed in similar projects (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Underestimating the time a task needs can express overestimation of what one can accomplish in that time; an unduly narrow completion window also expresses overprecision. Planning fallacy is therefore an application, rather than a fourth form alongside those in @tbl-confidence-calibration. The **outside view** begins with a reference class and then adjusts only for differences that are genuinely predictive (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Lovallo & Kahneman, 2003).

In Monty Hall, seeing two unopened doors can make staying and switching look equally promising. Yet the host’s rule for revealing a goat determines what the reveal tells us: similar-looking endings can carry different evidence. In the standard Monty Hall protocol, a knowledgeable host always reveals a goat behind an unchosen door and always offers a switch; if either goat door could be opened, assume the host chooses between them uniformly at random. Following the unchosen-door branch in @fig-monty-hall-protocol shows why switching wins with probability $2/3$, compared with $1/3$ for staying (Selvin, 1975). If the host instead opens doors or offers a switch selectively, the evidence changes. Likewise, “at least one child is a boy,” “the older child is a boy,” and a parent volunteering “I have a boy” arise from different sampling rules. The transferable question is not the puzzle answer but: **How was this information generated?**

The dated entries in @tbl-probability-forecast-ledger matter because memory rounds forecasts toward outcomes. “We knew it might fail” can describe almost any vague prior statement. A dated number, event definition, and update rule allow learning to survive hindsight.
@fig-risky-decision-map shows the first calculation: the lottery’s average utility lies below the utility of its average wealth.

A risk-preference measure seems useful because it could help predict choices beyond the task. Yet changing the task can change a person’s classification. Before using that label in another setting, we need to identify what the task measured. @tbl-risk-elicitation pairs each task with what it can reveal and what complicates the inference. A model maps choices back to a parameter, but comprehension, probability format, reference point, response mode, and noise can also affect the result.
Read @fig-prospect-theory-map from the two curves at the top to the risk attitudes below: the value of a gain or loss and the influence of its probability jointly shape the prediction.

We can now combine the two influences. Curvature describes the value of the possible gain or loss; weighting describes the influence of its probability. Crossing the gain–loss domain with the probability range in @tbl-prospect-fourfold gives four recurring patterns under commonly used parameterizations.

Many consequential decisions contain both. A physician can read trial evidence and also remember patients. A resident can see a flood map and also remember years without flooding. An investor can study a long return series and still give special weight to the market experienced during early adulthood. The independent dimensions in @fig-decision-experience-states make room for all four combinations, including having neither source. When both are present, disagreement calls for investigation; neither is automatically superior.

Hertwig and Wulff (2022) organize risk situations by asking whether description and experience are present or absent. The responses in @tbl-experience-states follow from what is missing: a selective history calls for broader evidence, while a described distribution may need a clearer, more usable presentation.

The slowly falling one-percent curve in @fig-experience-rare-event-sampling shows why an uneventful sample can coexist with a real rare-event risk. The following sections examine how selective exposure, stopping, and memory shape the experienced record.

Reviewing the four cells in @tbl-process-outcome prevents a successful result from excusing a poor process or a bad result from condemning a sound one. Hindsight, self-serving attribution, and rationalization make this separation difficult. People can sincerely explain choices whose causes they did not notice (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Johansson et al., 2005), so a retrospective account needs something firmer than memory to compare with.

The worked example in @fig-discount-model-crossover shows **dynamic inconsistency**: a plan that looks best from a distance can lose when temptation or effort becomes immediate. O'Donoghue and Rabin (1999) show how present bias can produce two familiar failures:

Waiting is rarely just empty time. @fig-intertemporal-choice traces how uncertainty, weak future imagery, and friction can obstruct the path to a delayed benefit. The distinctions in @tbl-22-delay-mechanisms broaden the diagnosis to include urgent needs, subjective time, and the emotions experienced while waiting:

Waiting is rarely just empty time. @fig-intertemporal-choice traces how uncertainty, weak future imagery, and friction can obstruct the path to a delayed benefit. The distinctions in @tbl-22-delay-mechanisms broaden the diagnosis to include urgent needs, subjective time, and the emotions experienced while waiting:

Before trying to make someone more patient, check whether the way the options are described changes the comparison. The classroom mnemonic **MOST** in @tbl-most-discounting keeps four option attributes visible, so that a change in wording or scale is not mistaken for a change in patience:
The choice “€100 today or €120 in a month” hides two complete outcome streams. The fuller representation in @fig-hidden-zero-frame makes the forgone payment at each date explicit:

A multiple price list seems to turn patience into a number: at which row does a person switch from a smaller-sooner to a larger-later amount? But choosing the earlier payment could also keep an urgent bill paid or avoid a promise the person distrusts. Treating either constraint as impatience would point to the wrong remedy. The design responses in @tbl-discount-identification show what must be measured or held comparable before attributing the observed choice to time preference.
Before choosing, use @tbl-intertemporal-time-stream to sketch what each option creates before, during, and after the focal event:

Mental accounting describes how people organize financial activities into accounts, code entries as gains or losses, and decide what to evaluate together (Thaler, 1985, 1999). @fig-mental-accounting-map follows these operations into valuation, where the same boundary can support a goal or hide a valuable alternative.

But a notional budget can become nonfungible. Someone may reject a worthwhile theatre ticket because the entertainment budget was used on a sports event, yet buy it after an equally costly medical expense or after receiving the sports ticket as a gift. Heath and Soll (1996) used such comparisons to show category-sensitive spending. @tbl-mental-budgets reports the study's **$50 prior-expense condition**. Each entry is the percentage showing the predicted “no after a prior purchase, yes after receiving that item as a gift, yes after an unrelated expense” pattern, averaged across four unrelated-expense controls.

The two panels of @fig-mental-accounting-evidence-redraw separate when an investor closes an account from the horizon over which returns are evaluated. Choose an evaluation horizon that matches the decision horizon and still permits disciplined review.

A budget helps protect money for a purpose, yet the same boundary can make a worthwhile purchase seem unaffordable while funds sit elsewhere. The audit needs to preserve the useful protection and expose the costly restriction. Use @tbl-mental-accounting-audit to reconstruct the decision twice, comparing the existing account with the alternatives and future costs that its boundary may hide:

The dashed arrow in @fig-habit-loop represents learning across repetitions, as the cue becomes associated with the action (Wood & Neal, 2007). Reward or relief can encourage that repetition, but neither is required every time the habit is performed. The association is not defined by how pleasurable the outcome is (Wood & Rünger, 2016), which helps explain why the student can keep checking social media without finding anything interesting.

Lally and colleagues (2010) followed people trying to establish everyday behaviors in a consistent context. The schematic curve in @fig-habit-formation-curve represents the diminishing gains in reported automaticity, while the range beneath it shows how widely the modeled time to approach a plateau varied. The median modeled time to reach 95% of the plateau was 66 days, with estimates from 18 to 254 days among participants whose data fitted the curve well.[^ch21-plateau]

The contrast between wanting and liking in @fig-wanting-liking suggests what the student could record: what checking seemed to offer, what happened immediately, and how it affected the work afterward. Comparing these records can help him choose a change that addresses what the checks actually provide.

The first three panels of @fig-reward-prediction-error-shift contrast these learning signals. Its separate fourth panel proposes informative progress cues as a task-design hypothesis, rather than a result established by those recordings. The distinction between motivational attraction and pleasure rests on further evidence (Berridge & Robinson, 1998).

The prompts in @tbl-20-brain turn a brief pause into an opportunity to notice the urge and choose a response.[^ch21-brain] The curve in @fig-urge-wave-observation shows one possible course, rather than a timetable to follow: the person can choose an action while the urge is still present.

The prompts in @tbl-20-brain turn a brief pause into an opportunity to notice the urge and choose a response.[^ch21-brain] The curve in @fig-urge-wave-observation shows one possible course, rather than a timetable to follow: the person can choose an action while the urge is still present.
@fig-well-being-six-lenses makes the central discipline visible: **do not move between measures without saying so**. A decision can look successful through one lens and costly through another.

Having followed the job through prediction, choice, experience, and reflection, use @tbl-well-being-targets to keep the questions separate. A strong answer in one row cannot silently stand in for the others.
The contrasts in @tbl-relational-well-being prevent the amount of contact from standing in for its quality or the support it provides:

The split between groups in @fig-income-wellbeing-evidence-synthesis shows why one average curve can conceal differences in the relationship. The comparison also remains sensitive to modeling choices. A later reanalysis estimated where the income–well-being curve could bend and found a different plateau pattern (Bennedsen, 2024). The useful lesson is to examine the measure, sample, and model before turning a fitted threshold into a rule for a person’s life.

The jobs can rank differently on pay, daily experience, purpose, and relationships. A single overall impression can hide which sacrifice produces the apparent advantage. Compare the options across the four fields in @tbl-well-being-decision-audit so that gains in one area can be weighed against sacrifices in another and checked at the later review. Complete one line in each cell; add detail only where it could change the decision.

In @tbl-price-war, if Firm 2 chooses a high price, Firm 1 earns 15 by choosing low rather than 10 by choosing high. If Firm 2 chooses low, Firm 1 earns 5 by choosing low rather than 2 by choosing high. Low is therefore Firm 1's best response to either action. The same reasoning holds for Firm 2. The unique Nash equilibrium is low–low, with payoffs 5,5, even though both firms would earn more at high–high.

[Behavioral Game Theory](24-behavioral-game-theory-equilibrium-is-a-benchmark-not-a-portrait.qmd#chapter-24-start) investigates the unresolved questions in the right-hand column of @tbl-equilibrium-boundary (Camerer, 2003): how do real people form beliefs, and how many steps of strategic reasoning do they use?

Both players could gain more by pursuing the stag together. Yet each risks being left with little if the other hunts hare. Agreement about the better joint outcome is therefore insufficient: each needs enough confidence that the other will follow through. The **stag hunt** in @tbl-stag-hunt makes that strategic uncertainty visible:

Before choosing a move, identify the structure of dependence. The branches in @fig-strategic-situation-diagnostic are strategic archetypes, not mutually exclusive categories. Mixed motives combine cooperation and conflict; anti-coordination is a coordination family in which players benefit from taking different rather than matching roles. Let the specified payoffs determine which features coexist.

Use the questions in @tbl-strategic-structures to identify which dependence needs attention, because the same visible behavior can arise from different games. Two firms may keep prices high because costs increased, because demand changed, because they independently reached the same best response, or because they coordinated illegally. Two colleagues may remain silent because they agree, fear authority, expect the other to speak, or each hopes the other will bear the cost. Surface behavior does not identify the payoff structure or the beliefs behind it.

Buyers and sellers may stand to gain from trade yet fail to find acceptable terms. Compare the rules in @tbl-market-institutions: each changes who can move, when they move, what they observe, and how a price is formed, with implications for whether the gains from trade are realized.

To predict the first round, we can ask which choices would be mutual best responses, or model how players actually reason about one another. To explain change across rounds or populations, we also need an account of how ways of playing become more common. The three branches in @fig-three-lenses-strategic-behavior keep these tasks distinct: finding mutual best responses, explaining a player’s reasoning, and tracing population change.

The number game rewards anticipating the group, but knowing the equilibrium does not tell a player how far others have reasoned. A model of limited strategic depth supplies a prediction between random choice and fully matched equilibrium beliefs. The ladder in @fig-level-k-reasoning-ladder illustrates a level-*k* model: each strategic level responds to the preceding level, starting from a specified nonstrategic anchor (Nagel, 1995; Stahl & Wilson, 1995). Behavioral game theory uses such models as disciplined alternatives to treating equilibrium as a literal description of first-round play (Camerer, 2003; Crawford et al., 2013).
Comparing the means, modes, and fitted reasoning depths in @tbl-beauty-contest-groups shows how the distribution a player needs to anticipate varies across settings and participant pools.
The distinctions can now be collected in @tbl-three-strategic-lenses. Choose a lens by the question it answers: a stable profile, a player’s reasoning, or change in a population.

Begin with what the action achieves for the employee. If it is a deliberate response to what colleagues do or expect, a strategic-reasoning model may help. If the question is how the routine spreads, compare the four processes in @tbl-strategy-diffusion-diagnostic and the evidence that would separate them:

In @tbl-one-shot-pd, if Player 2 cooperates, Player 1 receives 6 by defecting instead of 4 by cooperating. If Player 2 defects, Player 1 receives 2 by defecting instead of 0 by cooperating. Defection is therefore a dominant strategy for both players, and Defect–Defect is the unique Nash equilibrium. Yet Cooperate–Cooperate gives both a higher payoff.

Begin with the repeated-interaction branch of @fig-cooperation-architecture by adding a future to the opening game. If that changes the prediction, we can explain cooperation without yet changing what players value.

One recurring condition is **positive assortment**: cooperators interact with other cooperators more often than random mixing would predict. The explanation must then specify how partners are encountered or selected. The five rules in @tbl-five-rules separate how relatedness, repeated encounters, reputation, and population structure can support cooperation (Nowak, 2006).

The two panels in @fig-watched-eyes-evidence-update keep that field result beside the later cumulative evidence: two meta-analyses found no reliable overall increase in generosity from artificial surveillance cues (Northover et al., 2017). The next question is when a cue alters perceived observability, for whom, and with what consequence. [Appendix G](../appendices/appendix-f-when-evidence-breaks.qmd#a-concrete-update-watched-eyes-and-the-honesty-box) uses this case to show how a memorable result should be revised as evidence accumulates.

Removing rejection does not remove the rest of the setting. Anonymity, earned entitlement, experimenter observation, and whether the menu allows taking as well as giving can change the meaning of the action. The progression across @fig-social-preference-games-redraw shows which rights and options change between games; these contrasts narrow the explanation without turning a transfer into a pure measure of generosity.

A person can dislike inequality even when no one else expects sharing; that private concern is a social preference. Another person may keep all the money while believing that others would approve of sharing. In that case, a norm belief is outweighed by another motive. To explain or change the choice, distinguish what the person values from what they expect others to do or approve. @tbl-preference-norm separates these influences from rewards and sanctions, matching each to the evidence needed to identify it.

@tbl-cooperation-mechanisms compares features of an interaction that can change the incentive to cooperate. These features can coexist: a repeated relationship can also have a reputation system and formal enforcement. Use the comparison to identify what would change the prediction, rather than treating every cooperative act as evidence of generosity.

Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler (1986) asked separate samples of respondents to judge market practices. @fig-fairness-entitlements-redraw shows four selected historical vignettes. The car questions hold the size of the price increase at $200 but vary its relation to list price: one adds a surcharge above list, while the other removes a discount below list.[^ch25-fairness-vignettes]

Asch-type conformity varies across periods, cultures, tasks, and response conditions (Bond & Smith, 1996). Use @fig-asch-line-comparison to distinguish your own visual judgment from the response you would give after hearing a unanimous group.

**Conformity** describes movement toward a group pattern. The committee’s nods illustrate the distinction in @tbl-social-alignment-mechanisms: learning something and withholding a doubt can produce the same public agreement.

In the focus theory of normative conduct, a **descriptive norm** reports what people do, while an **injunctive norm** reports what people approve or disapprove of (Cialdini et al., 1990). The two branches in @fig-norm-message-diagnostic matter because a message can condemn a behavior while advertising that it is common. A late-night email may reveal that many colleagues work late without showing that they approve of the expectation. Silence in a meeting may reveal what people publicly do without revealing what they privately believe.

The parallel routes in @fig-social-pathways show why convergence alone cannot identify either a cascade or conformity pressure. An informational cascade can arise because earlier actions appear informative even when dissent is safe. Normative conformity can arise because disagreement is socially costly even when nobody thinks the majority knows more. The routes can interact, but the evidence needed to test them differs.

Popularity may reflect quality and partly produce the success later used to validate it. The experimental comparison in @fig-cultural-market-study-redraw helps separate those directions by comparing conditions with and without visible download counts, something an ordinary bestseller list cannot do.
Use @tbl-22-1 to audit the cue behind an apparent consensus before treating the consensus as additional evidence.

The two outcomes in @fig-social-learning-culture show why observation and imitation do not automatically produce useful accumulation. Accumulation also requires some source of variation or innovation, sufficient transmission and retention, and processes that preserve, select, or correct practices across learners or generations. The mixture differs across settings.

The family scene in @fig-personal-mimicry-crossed-arms illustrates similar postures without establishing who copied whom. @fig-mimicry-study-redraw instead compares behavior under different partner conditions, with stronger evidence for the face-rubbing contrast than for foot shaking.

The family scene in @fig-personal-mimicry-crossed-arms illustrates similar postures without establishing who copied whom. @fig-mimicry-study-redraw instead compares behavior under different partner conditions, with stronger evidence for the face-rubbing contrast than for foot shaking.

The first two claims in @fig-finance-euro-efficiency do not automatically establish the third. A price can be difficult to beat and still differ from a later estimate of fundamental value. Conversely, a price can be noisy without offering a low-risk implementable profit.

@fig-behavioral-finance-audit separates explaining a return pattern from establishing whether it survives realistic trading conditions and new observations. An **event study** measures returns around a defined event against a stated expected-return model. The [optional research track](#advanced-research-track-auditing-an-event-study) shows how to audit its timing, comparison, and uncertainty, using earnings announcements as an example.
The separate paths in @fig-asset-bubble-feedback allow a boom to begin with genuine innovation and later acquire a feedback component. Credit can amplify buying, but the loop does not require it.

Different strategies can sustain the same path. Passive trading can remain broadly consistent with fundamental value; feedback trading can follow price changes; a speculator may buy above a current value estimate when expecting a still higher next price. Haruvy and Noussair's (2006) rule classified behavior only when a trader's highest consistency score reached at least 8 of 15 periods; ties received fractional weights. Across 18 sessions with nine inexperienced participants each, the 162 trader classifications in @tbl-bubble-strategies split across several patterns:

The mixture in @fig-bubble-trader-strategies-redraw shows several patterns of trading within the same market. They help organize competing explanations for the price path, without establishing that every trader assigned a label used the same reasoning.

A rising price can reflect improving prospects, a reinforcing trading process, or both. Treating every rise as confirmation of a bubble would make the diagnosis impossible to correct; dismissing every concern as innovation could leave growing exposure unchecked. Use both evidence columns in @tbl-bubble-dashboard to record what makes the price look fragile, what could justify it, and which observation would change your assessment. A probability can help when the event and horizon are well defined.

If prices incorporate a clean public surprise rapidly, abnormal returns should cluster near the release. The delayed separation of the curves in @fig-finance-event-study-drift can illustrate slow updating, but an observed pattern like this could also reflect a weak benchmark, overlapping news, trading frictions, or sample construction that would not have been available in real time.

Read each row of @tbl-finance-anomalies from the historical finding through the behavioral possibility to the rival account: a familiar label alone cannot identify the mechanism or establish an implementable trade.

For Lena’s team, the next step is to distinguish the causes hidden by the shared silence. Each card in @fig-silence-mechanisms pairs a diagnostic question with a safeguard: collecting independent judgments addresses a different failure from assigning responsibility for action.
Use @tbl-group-failure-pathways to select the next observation and action. Several pathways may coexist, so record what each safeguard is expected to change.
